new_statements.rule_in_words: Second-hand: primary stress falls on the first long (heavy) vowel of the word; if there is none, on the first syllable. Secondary stress is placed from the opposite (right) edge (code Ed). Weight is partly a matter of vowel quality (schwa syllables are light) and every word contains at least one non-light syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Goedemans code (Ed): secondary stress is located at, or footed from, the edge opposite the main stress. No first-hand statement seen.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated in Goedemans; the entry is flagged '(QS: vowel quality, a word never consists of only light syllables)'. Breen 1976 (snippet) allows that stress may be phonemic.
new_statements.domain_note: Survey classification of the word-level pattern; no example words. Goedemans' own caveat (p.235) that entries deduced from limited material may be misplaced. The '(QS: vowel quality...)' note signals that the relevant weight is vowel quality (full vowel vs schwa), not only length; Jones 2000 (snippet) reports Breen 1992:10-11 as saying the syllable before a primary-stressed syllable has schwa, i.e. primary stress can be non-initial with pretonic reduction. Breen 1976 (snippet, first-hand) says only that 'length and/or stress may also be phonemic' and gives alternations like [núrmanand] vs [núrəmnándāgəl]; Black 1980:198 (on file) adds 'Stress is not transcribed for Kukatj, although Breen notes that it could conceivably be contrastive.'
new_statements.identity_note: Gugadj (Glottolog name) = Kukatj (AIATSIS G28, Breen's and Black's spelling), ISO ggd, Glottolog guga1239; a Paman language of the lower Flinders River near Normanton, not to be confused with Kukatja (kuka1246, Western Desert) or the Kokatha of South Australia. All sources examined describe this one variety (Breen's own corpus, one main speaker); Goedemans' 'Kukatj (T178)' is the same language.
